A study of more than 844,000 people across four countries found that relying on body mass index (BMI) alone can both overestimate and underestimate obesity, potentially exposing patients to inappropriate treatment.

Obesity diagnosis should move beyond a uniform BMI-based definition, researchers say, after analysing health data from 844,108 adults across China, the UK, the United States and Spain.

The findings, published in Nature on Wednesday, suggest that current methods of diagnosing obesity may fail to distinguish between people who are already experiencing health problems linked to excess body fat and those who face increased health risks but have no evidence of impaired organ function.

“People with obesity, like everyone else, deserve care matched to their needs: no less, and no more,” Professor Francesco Rubino, senior author of the study and chair of Metabolic and Bariatric Surgery at King's College London, said in a press release.

Currently, obesity is generally classified using body mass index (BMI), a measure calculated from a person's weight and height. However, BMI does not account for how much body fat a person has, where it is distributed or whether it is affecting their health.

In January 2025, a Commission published in The Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology proposed a new framework for diagnosing obesity, moving beyond BMI alone. It recommended distinguishing between two categories: clinical obesity, where excess body fat impairs organ function or everyday activities, and preclinical obesity, where excess body fat increases health risks but normal bodily function is preserved.

Researchers from King's College London and an international team of collaborators set out to test whether the proposed framework offered a more accurate way of identifying obesity and predicting health outcomes.

Their analysis found that BMI alone both overestimated and underestimated obesity across the four populations studied. Adding waist circumference and waist-to-height ratio to BMI assessments reduced these classification errors, with BMI alone missing obesity-level body fat in up to 8.6% of participants and incorrectly classifying up to 3.1% as having obesity.

The researchers also found that clinical obesity accounted for between 23% and 31% of all obesity cases, with an overall population prevalence of 5.6% to 10.9%.

Importantly, the two categories were associated with markedly different health outcomes. Clinical obesity was linked to a substantially higher risk of death, while preclinical obesity carried a more modest increase in risk.

Most people classified as having preclinical obesity at the start of the study — between 77% and 91% across the cohorts — did not progress to clinical obesity over a 10-year period.

“Body mass index alone cannot tell us whether someone is already ill or at risk of illness, or what care they need, leaving people vulnerable to both undertreatment and overtreatment,” Rubino said.

“Preclinical obesity should therefore be neither treated automatically as active disease nor dismissed as harmless. Some people may need preventive treatment, but its intensity should match their individual risk,” he added.

The researchers argue that the distinction could help healthcare professionals better identify who needs treatment for existing disease and who may benefit from preventive interventions, rather than applying the same approach to everyone with a high BMI.

“The marked differences in prognosis between clinical and pre-clinical obesity, consistently observed across countries and ethnic groups, support global adoption of the new framework to improve obesity care and policy worldwide," Professor An Pan, first author of the study from Huazhong University of Science and Technology in Wuhan, China, said.

According to a study, the end of the world was supposed to come on 13 November. It sounds dramatic and would be quite urgent – if the study were not already "outdated". Still, it is fascinating.

The so-called Doomsday study is already 66 years old, but it is probably the best-known study about the end of the world. In 1960 researchers used a mathematical formula to calculate the end of humankind for Friday 13 November 2026. The article with the provocative title "Doomsday: Friday, 13 November, A.D. 2026" was written by Austrian-American physicist Heinz von Foerster and his research team and published in the prestigious journal Science (source in German).

Key message and background of the Doomsday study

The researchers analysed historical data on the world population over the past two millennia and fitted a growth curve to it. Their projection was that if the then current growth rate of humans on Earth were extrapolated unchanged into the future, the curve would reach an infinite value in November 2026.

So by tomorrow, Friday, people would have multiplied to infinity. The mathematicians' logical conclusion was that on this day humanity would, purely in mathematical terms, "crush" itself through overpopulation.

The study caused a worldwide stir at the time, and that was exactly the intention. By pinning the date to a Friday the 13th, Heinz von Foerster mainly wanted to draw attention to the issue of overpopulation, which was being intensely debated then. Until the early 1990s the curve matched the actual figures remarkably well. After that global population growth slowed significantly, which is why current projections tend to expect stabilisation at around 10 billion people.

Why the "end of the world" is not happening

The world population is still growing, but more and more slowly. At first the number of people increased sharply because fewer were dying. Later families around the world began having fewer children. The fastest growth was in 1963, at more than two per cent per year. By 2020 this growth had fallen to below one per cent.

According to estimates by the United Nations (UN), the number of people on Earth will peak in the mid-2080s at about 10.3 billion. After that the world population will slowly start to decline again.

Friday is not the first predicted end of the world

As early as 1910 there was widespread panic about Halley's Comet. Newspapers warned of poisonous gases in its tail that could wipe out all life. Some traders exploited this fear and sold gas masks, protective pills or "comet umbrellas". But the comet passed and nothing happened.

Later there were repeated dates like this. A US radio preacher predicted Judgement Day for 21 May 2011. On 21 December 2012 a cycle of the Mayan calendar ended, which many also interpreted as the end of the world.

Even science has sometimes been wrong. In 1972 the study "Limits to Growth" warned that we would soon run out of vital raw materials. But people found new sources and solutions, and many commodities even became cheaper.

The problem with such predictions is always the same: past trends are simply projected into the future. This overlooks the fact that people respond to problems and adapt. That also applies to 13 November 2026. Humanity has developed differently from what was calculated 66 years ago.

So if you are now thinking you can finally tell your boss what you really think because everything will be over on Friday anyway, you might want to think again.

Announced annually by Travel + Leisure since 2014, India follows in the footsteps of previous destinations of the year including Brazil, Thailand and Costa Rica.

Once a key part of the hippie trail, India has been a major tourism destination for decades, drawing in the crowds for its wildlife, wellness practices and attractions like the iconic Taj Mahal.

In recent years, however, foreign arrivals have fallen, with 9.15 million in 2025, down 8% compared to its peak of 10.93 million in 2019.

India is hoping to change that, with a target of 100 million tourists a year by 2047, the centenary of the country's independence – and we imagine being named destination of the year for 2027 by Travel + Leisure will do more than a little to help.

Announced annually since 2014, recent destinations of the year have included Brazil in 2026, Thailand in 2025, and Costa Rica in 2024.

Writing about the South Asian country, Travel + Leisure editor-in-chief Jacqui Gifford said: “Certain destinations tug at the heartstrings more than others. For me, one of those places is India.

“I first visited when I was three and was spellbound by the colours, the buttery naan, the fine-spun silk of the saris, the chaos of the traffic, the warmth that emanates from every conversation. The country seeps into your skin.”

Where to go in India

Spanning some 3.29 million square kilometres split into 28 states and eight union territories, it can be difficult to know where to begin when planning a trip to India.

If you’re looking for a city break, Travel + Leisure suggests heading to Udaipur, India's very own “Venice of the East”.

Seven lakes surround the city, and you can explore sights like the City Palace or the Monsoon Palace. You can even stay in an actual palace, with the Taj Lake Palace regularly named among the best hotels in the world.

Alternatively, head to New Delhi for the Qutb Minar and Humayun’s Tomb, or as a stop before heading to the Taj Mahal in Agra.

Other destinations making the recommendations list include the Lakshadweep archipelago, where just a few islands open to tourists each year; Madhya Pradesh, where you’ll find India’s largest tiger population alongside spectacular temples; and the state of Chettinad, with its distinct architectural style.

An 11-month-old boy has been rescued alive after spending about 24 hours buried underground in a dog crate in the US state of South Carolina, where police say he was left by his father.

Koah Sharp was found on Tuesday in woodland on a neighbour’s property, crying and covered in dirt, his grandfather John Comer told the Associated Press news agency on Wednesday.

Soon afterwards, the baby stopped crying, and once he had been lifted on to the back of a truck, he sat up.

“I became ecstatic, my hands straight in the air. I’m looking in the sky, jumping up and down, praising God,” John Comer said. “And at the same time I hit my knees and I’m just crying.”

Koah is expected to make a full recovery, Lexington County Sheriff Jay Koon said after leaving hospital.

The boy’s father, 25-year-old Michael Comer, has been charged with attempted murder. He has been in custody since Monday, the day Koah went missing, and was arrested while hiding in a building in the town of Batesburg-Leesville.

Authorities have not given any details of a possible motive. It was not immediately clear whether Michael Comer has a lawyer who could respond to the charges. A court hearing was scheduled for Thursday.

Freshly disturbed soil and cries from underground

Dozens of emergency workers searched the countryside for the boy with reddish-blond hair. After a full day, they found freshly disturbed soil and heard crying coming from beneath the ground, Koon said.

“As you can imagine, the race was on. Everyone was trying to get him out,” the sheriff said.

He said Koah had probably survived thanks to cool temperatures and an air pocket created by a towel wrapped around the buried crate. When rescuers freed him, the boy was “clinging to life”, Koon added.

“We’re better now that we know that Koah is safe,” said his great-aunt, Amber Hammond, who watched as he was pulled from the crate.

Taken before a carer arrived

According to authorities, Koah had been in the care of Michael Comer’s mother. She left the boy with her son while she ran an errand, as another carer was on the way.

“By the time the caregiver got there, Michael was gone, and Koah was gone with him,” Koon said.

Surveillance footage from several local businesses showed Michael Comer without the baby on Monday afternoon, the sheriff added.

John Comer said he had taken in his son and grandson on Monday, after Michael Comer told him they needed somewhere to stay. He now feels his son took advantage of him, he said, but he is grateful he agreed: if they had gone elsewhere, Koah might not have been found in time.

“It just seems like he already had this planned out, and he knew what he was doing,” he said. “And he took the opportunity to do what he did. And if it hadn’t have been here, I don’t think anybody would have known where he would have went, and this would be a completely different story.”

Hammond said her nephew had talked about taking the baby to New York because “he didn’t want to be in the same state as the mom”. When Koah disappeared, she and other relatives assumed Michael Comer had handed him over to someone.

“We had no idea something like this would happen at all,” she said.

Koah’s parents “have had some situations”, Koon said. “Children,” he added, “sometimes get caught in the middle.”

In October, Michael Comer was sentenced to probation after pleading guilty to domestic violence and aggravated breach-of-the-peace charges over an arrest in July, according to Lexington County court records. Prosecutors dropped a gun charge as part of a plea deal, and he was credited with more than two months already spent in jail.

Hammond, who looked after Koah last weekend, said he had been trying to stand on his own and loved watching Mickey Mouse cartoons.

John Comer said he had never heard his grandson cry before he was found underground.

“He’s always been happy,” he said. “The kid’s always got a smile on his face.”

Europe sweeps a new ranking of the world’s quietest cities, with Italian destinations featuring three times in the top 10. Here’s where to go to escape the noise.

According to research by Avanti Travel Insurance, European destinations dominate a new ranking of the world’s quietest cities to visit in 2027, claiming all spots in the top 10.

German, Finnish, Dutch and other Nordic graduates are not interested in EU careers, as new figures from the EPSO competition show that northern Europeans are largely staying away. Is Brussels doing enough to compete with stronger national labour markets?

The EU faces a shortage of northern European staffers. Out of roughly 33,000 employees in European Commission administrator posts, only 1,370 are German and 380 are Dutch. Sweden has 264 workers, and both Denmark and Finland have fewer than 200. The numbers will decrease even more as eurocrats retire, and there is no generational renewal in sight.

The European Personnel Selection Office (EPSO) attracted 174,727 applicants to its 2026 AD5 generalist competition, but while Italy accounted for almost half of all candidates, Germany, Sweden, Denmark and the Netherlands registered comparatively few applications. Germany, the EU's most populous member state, produced just 11,699 applicants, compared with Italy's 79,343. Sweden registered only 1,804 candidates, while Denmark attracted fewer than 1,000.

"Ideally, we would like each member state to be represented proportionally across all EU Institutions. The Commission should consider launching competitions specifically for underrepresented member states", suggested Monika Hohlmeier, an EPP MEP from Germany's Christian Democrats.

She also pointed out that, in many sectors, "EU salaries are [actually] lower". For graduates in Germany, Denmark, Sweden and the Netherlands, an EU career is not necessarily more attractive than the opportunities available in their national labour markets.

Better opportunities at home

According to Eurostat, 90.6% of recent graduates in Germany and 90.1% in the Netherlands were employed in 2025, compared with an EU average of 83%. Employment among recent university graduates also exceeded 90% in Sweden.

Germany offers particularly strong private-sector alternatives. Graduates in engineering, finance, law and economics can pursue careers in major companies, banks, consultancies and technology firms, with starting salaries reaching €55,000 to €70,000 gross annually.

The public sector also offers competitive opportunities. In Germany, graduates can qualify for positions on the A13 salary scale, with basic monthly salaries of €4,500 to €5,300 or more, depending on the employer and salary step. Permanent civil servants also benefit from job security, pensions and healthcare support.

By comparison, newly recruited EU officials at the AD5 level can receive approximately €4,749 net per month, rising to around €5,734 with an expatriation allowance — not attractive enough to convince northern European graduates to relocate and undergo EPSO's lengthy selection process.

"The recruitment process is unfortunately often very long and some graduates may search for other opportunities before hearing back from an EU Institution on the status of their application. There is also a need to align the salary structure and entry-level pay grades with competitive rates that match market rates, especially in specialty areas such as IT, economics or law. At the moment, EU salaries are often lower", said Hohlmeier.

Working conditions are another factor. Denmark's standard full-time working week is usually commonly 37 hours, while Sweden and Germany offer established systems of paid leave, parental benefits and employment protections. EU institutions also provide generous leave and employment benefits, but joining them means adapting to a different administrative environment and potentially working in a second or third language.

Candidates must also consider housing costs, the loss of professional networks and separation from family and friends. For graduates with partners, children or financial commitments, the advantages of an EU career may not outweigh the costs of moving abroad.

They must also prepare for competitive examinations and may face a lengthy wait before receiving an offer. Even securing a place on an EPSO reserve list does not guarantee employment, making the process less appealing.

Southern Europeans see an actual opportunity

The situation is very different in southern Europe, where weaker employment prospects, stagnant wages and job insecurity make Brussels look like a haven. According to Eurostat, just 71.8% of recent graduates in Italy and 62.4% in Greece were employed in 2025, compared with the EU's 83% average.

Low salaries are not the only problem. These countries also have low starting salaries, limited promotion opportunities and jobs that fail to provide the financial security their qualifications promised.

Italy is a prime example. The OECD found that Italian wages remained 6.1% below early-2021 levels in the first quarter of 2026, the largest decline among major OECD economies. Young professionals also face unpaid or poorly paid internships, temporary contracts and freelance arrangements with fewer employment protections.

Spain recorded the EU's highest unemployment rate in 2025, at 10.5%. Although labour reforms reduced the share of fixed-term workers from 24.8% in early 2022 to 14.8% in early 2026, the growing use of permanent-seasonal contracts still leaves some workers facing periods without predictable earnings.

Spanish wages also remained 2% below early-2021 levels in the first quarter of 2026. For young professionals in Madrid, Barcelona and other expensive cities, employment does not necessarily guarantee affordable housing or financial security.

Greece recorded 8.9% unemployment in 2025 and the EU's lowest recent-graduate employment rate. Graduates seeking careers outside tourism, hospitality and other lower-paid services face limited opportunities, while housing costs add further pressure. Furthermore, according to Eurostat, 26.4% of Greece's population spent at least 40% of disposable household income on housing in 2025, compared with an EU average of 7.7%.

So for graduates in these countries, an EU career offers a major improvement in earnings and job security. Entry-level public servants with university degrees in Italy, Spain and Greece can earn between €780 and €1,800 net per month, considerably lower than the approximately €4,749 available to a newly recruited AD5 official without an expatriation allowance.

According to Hohlmeier, "among young people educated people with a bachelor’s degree, unemployment is higher in Spain, Italy and Greece compared to northern countries, so this could play a role. Perhaps students from these countries are more willing to take a risk and apply. Perhaps there is also better word of mouth in Spain, Italy and Greece about these opportunities."

Can Brussels reverse the trend?

This is a longer-term challenge for EU institutions, as they established a common selection process to recruit officials from across all member states.

Although recruitment is based on merit and application figures do not necessarily determine the nationality of successful candidates, persistently low participation from northern Europe makes it harder to address existing geographical imbalances as older officials retire. One of the solutions the Commission has come up with is action plans aimed at attracting candidates from underrepresented member states, but even these will fail when there are simply not enough applicants.

"As a member of the Budgetary Control Committee, I welcome any effort by the Commission to attract applicants from under-represented countries, since it is our common goal for all member states to be represented proportionally. We need geographical balance and proportionate representation of all member states in all EU Institutions including not just the Commission, but also the Agencies and other institutions", said Hohlmeier.

She added that "competitions specifically for under-represented countries could help with this. I think at the end of the day, it is up to the individual to decide if this is a career path they would like to pursue and if it is truly their passion. It takes a lot of consideration, because it involves moving to a different country, often learning new languages, understanding local bureaucracies and cultures, and living far from friends and family."

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has urged Brussels to stand firm on the EU's carbon market reforms and reject further changes to its second phase, signalling Berlin's opposition to reopening a hard-fought political compromise on carbon pricing, according to a letter seen by Euronews.

"It is extraordinarily important that the EU ensures investment certainty in emissions trading," reads the letter.

The intervention comes as the European Parliament and EU governments negotiate the European Commission's July 17 proposal to align the Emissions Trading System (ETS) with the bloc's 2040 climate target.

The reform has become increasingly contentious, with several EU countries seeking to weaken or even scrap parts of the system, blaming carbon pricing for high electricity costs.

Merz warned that businesses need predictable carbon prices to make long-term investment decisions, and that uncertainty risks undermining investment in Europe's energy and industrial sectors.

His stance contrasts with that of his own Economy and Energy Minister, Katherina Reiche, who has pushed to relax carbon rules and extend free emissions allowances for industry.

The ETS, the EU's carbon market, requires power generators and energy-intensive industries to pay for their greenhouse gas emissions. However, some heavy industries receive free allowances to help them cope with the costs of decarbonisation and international competition.

Merz called on Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to conclude the ongoing reform swiftly, citing competitiveness concerns without weakening the carbon market.

"European companies in the energy and industrial sectors have built their business models on the expectation of reliable CO2 price signals," the letter says.

He argued that the impact of carbon pricing on electricity bills should be addressed through existing compensation mechanisms rather than changes to the ETS itself.

These mechanisms allow governments to offset indirect carbon costs faced by electricity-intensive industries, helping to protect European manufacturing.

Merz rejects further changes to ETS2

Merz took an even firmer line on ETS2, the EU's second carbon market, which is due to take effect in 2028 and will extend carbon pricing to fuels used in road transport and heating buildings.

He argued that the compromise reached in early 2026 to delay its introduction until 2028, alongside measures to stabilise prices, should be sufficient to keep costs under control.

The German Chancellor rejected any further adjustments and insisted that negotiations on ETS1 and ETS2 must remain separate.

His position could put Berlin at odds with governments seeking further concessions on ETS2, particularly those concerned about the political and social impact of higher fuel and heating costs on households.

Several member states have called for additional delays or changes to ETS2's price-stabilisation mechanism, which allows more emissions allowances to enter the market if carbon prices rise too sharply.

Berlin draws a red line on carbon pricing

Merz's intervention comes amid mounting pressure on the EU to soften its climate policies in response to concerns over industrial competitiveness and household energy bills.

While acknowledging that industry needs protection from high electricity costs, the Chancellor wants that support delivered through compensation mechanisms rather than by weakening the carbon price signal that underpins the ETS.

His letter amounts to a warning against allowing political pressure over energy costs to trigger a broader retreat from the EU's carbon market.

Reacting to the letter, Linda Kalcher, executive director of the think tank Strategic Partnerships, said Merz's direct intervention "carries real weight".

“His letter sends an unmistakable signal: a robust ETS is vital for industrial competitiveness and future investment. So I expect Germany — and him — to step up and lead to help broker an agreement in December,” Kalcher said.

After the European Parliament votes in plenary in mid-December, political talks among the EU co-legislators will start.

NASA’s Dart spacecraft deliberately slammed into little Dimorphos in 2022 to see whether such a defensive move might help save Earth from a killer space rock one day.

Next month, the small car-sized Hera, launched in 2024, will venture even closer — just 20 kilometres away.

The Dart spacecraft — short for Double Asteroid Redirection Test — sent rubble and even boulders flying off Dimorphos, providing an extra kick to the impact’s momentum. The debris trail extended thousands of miles (more than 10,000 kilometres) into space for months.

Some of that debris could still be in the vicinity, according to scientists.

Dimorphos is an estimated 500 feet (151 meters) in diameter. Didymos is roughly 2,560 feet (780 meters) in diameter.

The US wants to turn Pax Silica, its AI supply chain alliance, into a wider economic security pact, to be endorsed in San Francisco on Sunday. EU countries have raised concerns, citing vague definitions, a terminology clash over superintelligence and risks to their regulatory autonomy.

The US is facing resistance from the EU over plans to expand its global AI initiative, Pax Silica, into a broader economic security framework aimed at protecting American technological leadership.

The latest draft of a US declaration, discussed by EU ambassadors on Wednesday and seen by Euronews, states that “economic security is fundamental to national security, and that no nation can be secure without securing its critical systems and technologies from those that would do it harm.”

Washington wants members of Pax Silica, a US-led coalition designed to secure supply chains for AI, semiconductors and critical minerals, to endorse the declaration at a ceremony in San Francisco on Sunday.

The EU joined the initiative in June despite reservations from France, after several member states had already signed up individually. But Washington's latest proposals have revived divisions within the bloc.

The declaration calls for a “common understanding” on protecting sensitive technologies and critical infrastructure by diversifying supply chains and coordinating responses to economic coercion.

It goes further, arguing that “durable economic security among trusted partners rests not on professions of friendship alone, but on the vigilant protection of the foundations on which our economies depend and on the active promotion of shared innovation and technological leadership.”

The concerns are rooted partly in Washington's previous attempts to restrict access to advanced AI technology.

In 2025, the Biden administration introduced export controls under its AI Diffusion Framework that would have limited access to the most advanced AI chips for several EU countries.

The Trump administration scrapped the measures shortly before they were due to take effect, but they would have created serious problems for the EU's single market, which is built on the free movement of goods.

The restrictions were also seen as a signal that Washington did not consider some EU countries sufficiently aligned with its approach to China.

The US has sought to curb China's growing technological capabilities by preventing Chinese companies from accessing the most advanced AI chips, largely designed by American firms such as Nvidia.

One sticking point in the latest declaration is its broad definition of sensitive technologies and critical infrastructure.

Some EU member states are demanding objective criteria, fearing that the current wording would give Washington considerable discretion to impose restrictions and pressure its allies to follow suit.

Another dispute centres on terminology. Trump is pushing the concept of superintelligence, while the European Commission has proposed an explanatory note clarifying that the EU understands the term to mean artificial intelligence.

For Brussels, this is more than a semantic distinction. It is a question of legal certainty, given that AI is already defined in key EU legislation, notably the Artificial Intelligence Act.

Washington has long opposed the AI Act and is now proposing a Pax Silica working group to explore innovation-friendly regulatory approaches.

On Wednesday, EU governments gave the Commission a mandate to represent the bloc and negotiate the content of the declaration with the US. But the Commission might not receive a mandate to sign it in time for the San Francisco ceremony.

“We affirm that the safeguarding of these sensitive technologies and critical infrastructure is a shared endeavour; that the security of each signatory is strengthened by the vigilance of all; and that we engage in this common cause as trusted partners,” the text concludes.

Nvidia founder Jensen Huang is under investigation. What long-term impact could it have on AI and China?

Most affairs of the heart are kept private.

But for Nvidia founder Jensen Huang, his secret relationship has become public and that could have a global impact on artificial intelligence, as he is being investigated over his relationship with an alleged Chinese spy and whether he disclosed confidential intellectual property.

Nvidia designs the world’s most powerful chips and has become an AI infrastructure company, reaching its arm into robotics as well as autonomous driving. Nvidia has also invested in many AI companies across the world, including in Europe.

The chips that it produces run AI systems and have become an important front for the United States’ rivalry with China to lead in technology, with Washington even restricting access to the chips for Beijing.

Huang had lobbied for the US to relax its chip export rules to China.

"Nvidia is kind of at the base of [the AI ecosystem]," said Carmem Domingues, a former White House Senior AI Advisor to the Biden administration.

"All the AI companies either owe money to NVIDIA and/or depend on them to actually run the models and continue developing and growing their businesses," she told Euronews Next.

A new leader?

As Nvidia’s board reportedly considers ousting him, there are questions over whether the saga could bring about another 2008-style financial crisis and who could replace him.

Huang is Nvidia, he created the company three decades ago, his keynotes are attended by packed audiences and he has a celebrity fanbase that follows him wherever he goes.

As to who could replace him, Domingues believes "there's not someone who is sort of prepped and ready to go next in line".

Despite his two children being part of the company, "it's unclear what exactly their roles are in or how ready they would be to take over", and anyone else in the company seems "unlikely", she said.

Even if Huang was removed, they would likely keep him in some kind of role and that would be "in a way quote-unquote enough of a punishment for any potential wrongdoing", she added.

If you pin the two countries as adversaries, the fact that they would be spying on each other is kind of expected.

Shares in Nvidia fell about 8% in trading on the news that the company board was reportedly considering ousting him.

"All the AI companies… have this sort of roundabout funding of each other... So everything is very intertwined and disastrous in many ways. And one falling can bring down a lot," said Domingues.

In 2008, global financial services firm Lehman Brothers fell and took the hit, while many other companies were considered too big to fail.

"Would they [Nvidia] protect him [Huang] in the name of not letting the 'house of cards' fall down?... So is Jensen, in a way, too big to fail himself? In a way. Yes," said Domingues.

But the AI bubble was already showing signs of bursting long before the Huang news and the US midterm election results, which showed a backlash to data centres and AI.

"It's almost burst. We're looking at the past month and then the US election and looking at markets. And there are also other problems, other issues. For example, the data centres are struggling with infrastructure, with the power grids," said Sheikha Maytha Bint Maktoum, an investor and founder of mental health company MindFriend.

For her, many AI startup valuations are detached from business fundamentals.

"No book I have read could have prepared me to see a day where a company is completely built on something that could vanish tomorrow," she said.

"There’s a product, but you can copy that product, and that product has no revenue... it is at a loss and valued at $14 billion (€12.6 billion)."

But for Nvidia, she believes any financial disruptions to the company would be "temporary", as "Nvidia has for decades built such a strong infrastructure around this ecosystem, it’s very difficult for me to see that would have a long-term impact".

Impact on China?

The Huang story has mostly been framed in the West as a question of market stability: could trouble at Nvidia ripple through an AI economy built on circular funding?

But in China, the conversation tends to run in a different direction. Companies there have spent years trying to reduce reliance on American chips, and episodes like this reinforce the instinct.

For Chinese company Xynova, which makes robotic hands, the thinking is more around long-term independence.

"Usually Chinese companies want to be more independent, not rely on the supplies... if you have to rely on American companies for supply, then it’s a big bottleneck," Isabel Zhu of Xynova told Euronews Next at the Web Summit tech conference in Lisbon.

"Huawei... they are trying to develop the chips, they’re working so hard, and they advocate that they are the Nvidia in China."

In her personal opinion, the AI race only makes the country want to push harder.

"I have faith in Chinese companies. If you really want to do something, then that will happen," she said.

But for Domingues, the Huang investigation will not change anything in the so-called AI race.

Long before the Huang saga, she said it was already framed as an AI race, noting that the US AI Action Plan in 2025 is literally called "Winning the AI Race". So, the scandal will not change much.

"If you pin the two countries as adversaries, the fact that they would be spying on each other is kind of expected... Every movie about the Cold War is about a spy… I find it unlikely [that it would change the rhetoric]."

His margin of fewer than 5,000 votes caps a midterm wave that has handed Democrats control of both chambers of Congress.

Democrat Scott Colom has won the US Senate race in Mississippi, becoming the first Black senator elected from the southern US state in more than 140 years, US networks projected on Wednesday.

Colom, a 43-year-old district attorney, defeated Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith. It was perhaps the most remarkable seat flip of a midterm election in which Democrats won back the majority in both the Senate and the House of Representatives.

CNN, NBC and CBS called the race on Wednesday, eight days after election night. With about 99 per cent of the vote counted, Colom led Hyde-Smith by 49.2 per cent to 48.7 per cent, a margin of 4,585 votes.

“Mississippi, our prayers have often changed the course of history,” Colom told a jubilant crowd of supporters in Jackson, the state capital, on Wednesday night. “God didn’t want us to get it the easy way. He wanted us to get it the Mississippi way.”

In a prayerful, solemn speech, he paid tribute to Mississippi’s long tradition of Black activism and faith in progress.

He will also be the first Democratic senator from Mississippi in nearly 40 years.

Hyde-Smith, 67, who has held the seat since 2018, conceded in a video posted on X.

“While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters,” she said. “I want to congratulate Scott Colom and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state.”

A blow for Trump

The result in one of the most solidly Republican states deepens the setback for US President Donald Trump. Voters across the country turned away from his Republican Party, even in states that had not sent a Democrat to Washington in decades.

Democrats will now hold 55 seats in the 100-member Senate and Republicans 44. One race, in Alaska, has yet to be called.

Including Mississippi, Democrats flipped eight Republican-held Senate seats, with breakthroughs in South Carolina, North Carolina, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, Texas and Maine. Several of those seats had not changed hands for decades.

Control of both chambers of Congress gives Democrats the power to block legislation, investigate the administration and stop Trump’s appointments. The defeat also leaves the 80-year-old president as a lame duck for the final two years of his term.

The race went down to the wire, surprising many observers who had doubted how far the Democratic wave would reach. The wave was driven by mounting anger over Trump’s hardline immigration policy, the war in Iran and the rising cost of living.

“Blue Mississippi is here,” Chuck Schumer, the top Democrat in the Senate, wrote on X after the projections came in.

“Scott Colom is the only person who could’ve gotten this done. I knew it from the moment I met him.”

‘The power of prayer’

The first Black senator ever elected in the United States, Hiram Revels, was from Mississippi. He served during the Reconstruction era that followed the American Civil War.

In his speech, Colom described how Revels, a minister by training, used his powerful oratory to win the backing of other politicians for his run for the Senate.

“That’s an example of the power of prayer, and through our history, there are so many people that lifted this state up through the power of prayer in very dark times,” Colom said.

“It’s local people that have faith that Mississippi can make progress, and it’s local people like the people out here who had faith that we could win this election,” he added.

The rapper, who set a Guinness World Record for freestyle rapping in early November, says he "trained like an athlete" and burned around 3,000 calories during the event.

Imagine, first, freestyle rapping at all. If you can wrap your head around the art of spitting rhymes and punchlines on the fly, imagine doing it for more than eleven hours straight.

Then, imagine doing all the above while facing off against 250 competitors in 200 freestyle battles, and losing just three of them.

On 7 November, 24-year-old Spanish MC Gazir, who moonlights as a physics student at the University of Oviedo, set a Guinness World Record by completing 200 freestyle battles in under 12 hours – an effort that seems to defy the very subject he studies in his spare time.

When Gazir - born Gabriel Sánchez Poyal - speaks with Euronews Culture four days later, the first thing he does is apologise for his voice. It still hadn’t fully recovered.

“Every part of my body, my mind and even my soul was involved to make this possible,” he says.

In an ordinary freestyle competition, he explains, he might have three or four battles in a day. At Red Bull Gazir Contra Todos, held in his hometown of Gijón, he performed 50 times as many.

To complete the challenge, he had to finish within 12 hours and lose no more than 10 battles. He needed 11 hours, 23 minutes and 14 seconds, and he won 197 of them.

By the end of the event, he says, he was exhausted. Understandably. According to the fitness ring he was wearing, he had burned around 3,000 calories.

Training like an athlete

As Gazir explains, rapping is far more than an exercise of the mind.

In September and October, he followed a very particular schedule with the help of a personal trainer, nutritionist, psychologist and vocal specialists.

Preparing for the event was the biggest challenge he had ever undertaken, Gazir says. “My routine became like the routine of an athlete.”

He ate specially tailored meals at specific times, went to the gym and spent hours practising his freestyle technique. Some days, he trained with other rappers, using their insults and improvisations as inspiration. On others, he practised at home alone, rapping about household objects or whatever random topics he found online.

But the most important training revolved around his voice.

Freestyle battles are loud, high-energy contests involving rapid-fire exchanges. If you watch the video, he says, “it looks like I’m shouting all the time.”

Gazir worked with coaches to improve his breathing and projection so he could maintain his intensity for hours on end without damaging his vocal cords.

And he really means hours on end.

During the record attempt, he had just 20 seconds between each battle and a four-minute break after every 40 – barely enough time to catch his breath or eat a snack.

He drank water and isotonic drinks throughout, eating mashed bananas and other fruit during his short pauses. And he estimates he drank a few Red Bulls, too, keeping his energy sources pretty much all natural.

‘No limits to the imagination’

No amount of physical preparation could guarantee that Gazir would have something new to say when it came time to perform. “I didn’t plan anything,” he says when asked how he kept his rhymes fresh. “In freestyle, you have to improvise all the time.”

In each battle, the rappers traded four-bar verses, taking six turns apiece. Every insult, punchline or pun gave Gazir something new to work with, provided he could think of a comeback before his next turn. And after each battle, he had to start all over again.

“Maybe your voice has a limit, maybe your legs have a limit,” he says. “But if you are with the flow, with the energy of each battle, each bar, each moment, the imagination has no limits.”

Gazir won his first 115 battles before Babi finally defeated him in the 116th at 5:39pm – more than six hours after the marathon effort began.

He later lost to Skone and Bnet – two Spanish rappers and former world champions – but he finished with a victory over Mexico’s Aczino, a three-time winner of Red Bull Batalla, the world championship of Spanish-language freestyle rap.

That so many rappers came out to battle Gazir says a lot about the growth of freestyling in Spain and Latin America. Gazir, who has earned his living as a freestyler since he was about 17, says the Spanish scene is now a “mature” one, complete with professional leagues, national competitions and international tournaments.

As for his own ambitions, Gazir isn’t planning to retire to a recording studio just yet. He’s happy to keep competing, although his university courses provide a welcome distraction. “Sometimes it’s useful to disconnect from your routine,” he says about physics.

He is already considering another challenge, though, and it might somehow be even harder than his me-against-the-world marathon battle: learning to freestyle in English.

“It’s really difficult, but it will be a good challenge,” he admits.

“I will be making freestyle in English soon.”

Household electricity and gas prices in the EU fell in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period in 2025. Prices rose in many European capitals in October, and households could face higher bills in early 2027.

Even as the Iran war started driving up wholesale gas prices, household electricity and gas prices fell on average across the EU in the first half of 2026.

The differences between countries were striking. A unit of electricity cost more than three times as much in Ireland as in Hungary, according to Eurostat.

Where in Europe did households pay the most and least for electricity and gas? And how do the rankings change when local price levels are taken into account?

Among 38 European countries with data, household electricity prices including taxes ranged from €6.6 per 100 kWh in Turkey to €38.7 in Ireland in the first half of 2026. Hungary had the lowest price in the EU at €11.4, while the EU average was €28.3.

In euro terms, Ireland was followed by Germany (€36.2), Belgium (€35.8), Austria (€32.6), Italy (€31.4) and Sweden (€30.6), all above €30 per 100 kWh.

Electricity prices were lower than the EU average in Spain (€25.1) and France (€24.9).

Romania has the highest electricity prices in purchasing power terms

Prices were generally lower in EU candidate countries, and the gap with the most expensive countries was large. That gap narrowed once differences in local price levels were taken into account using purchasing power standards (PPS).

Electricity prices ranged from 12.6 PPS per 100 kWh in Iceland to 46.9 in Romania. Poland (41.1) and Czechia (34.3) rounded out the top three, followed by Ireland and Italy at 32.8 each.

After Iceland, Turkey (13.5), Malta (13.8), Hungary (14.7) and Norway (15.0) had the lowest prices in purchasing power terms.

Among the EU’s four largest economies, Italy had the highest price (32.8), closely followed by Germany (32.4). Spain (28.0) was close to the EU average (28.4), while France (23.3) was cheaper.

Electricity prices rose sharply in Romania

Household electricity prices fell by 2.2% on average in the EU compared with the second half of 2025. Measured in euros, Finland recorded the largest rise at 19.5%, followed by Turkey (11.2%), Poland (10.6%), Lithuania (10.6%) and Sweden (10.4%).

Denmark (-28.2%) and Luxembourg (-24.1%) recorded the biggest falls. Prices in Italy rose by 5.9%, while they fell by 6.5% in Germany, 6% in Spain and 3% in France.

Compared with the first half of 2025, the EU average electricity price fell by 1.6%. Romania recorded the biggest increase in euro terms at 51.9%, followed by Turkey (35%), Ireland (19.8%) and Finland (18.4%).

Prices fell in all four of the EU’s largest economies: France (-7%), Germany (-5.7%), Italy (-4.5%) and Spain (-3.9%).

Government policies help explain why price changes vary, according to Professor Xiaoyi Mu, director of the Centre for Energy, Petroleum and Mineral Law and Policy at the University of Dundee. Taxes, levies and network charges make up a large part of final prices. Denmark, for example, temporarily cut its electricity tax by roughly €0.10 per kWh from 1 January 2026. Finland had no such tax relief.

Energy market intelligence firm VaasaETT, which helps compile the Household Energy Price Index (HEPI), has also pointed to differences in the energy mix, tariff structures, how suppliers buy and price energy, and how costs are shared between groups of customers.

Sweden has the most expensive gas

Across the 29 European countries with data, household natural gas prices, including taxes, ranged from €1.6 per 100 kWh in Georgia to €22 in Sweden in the first half of 2026. Hungary (€3.3) had the lowest price in the EU, where the average was €11.

The Netherlands (€16.2), France (€13.5), Portugal (€12.6) and Austria (€12.4) rounded out the top five.

Gas prices were above the EU average in France, Germany (€11.6) and Italy (€11.4), and below it in Spain (€7.9).

In PPS terms, prices ranged from 4.3 per 100 kWh in Hungary to 20.8 in North Macedonia. North Macedonia was below the EU average in euro terms (€10.8) and moved to the top of the ranking once local price levels were taken into account.

Sweden (17.7), Portugal (15.0) and the Netherlands (13.8) also ranked among the most expensive. At the lower end, Turkey (5.0), Luxembourg (6.6) and Croatia (6.8) had the lowest prices after Hungary.

Household gas prices fell by 10.2% on average in the EU compared with the second half of 2025. In euro terms, Italy (-23.2%), Spain (-17.6%) and Greece (-16%) recorded the largest falls. Turkey had the biggest rise at 12.9%, followed by Romania (6.3%).

Compared with the first half of 2025, the EU average fell by 3.5%. France was the only one of the EU’s four largest economies where gas prices rose year on year, up 3.7%.

Why do wholesale price rises take time to reach households?

The figures cover only about four months after the US and Israel began striking Iran in late February. The full impact on household bills may take longer to show up.

“There is always a lag between the benchmark wholesale natural gas price (TTF) and the prices paid by households,” Xiaoyi Mu told Euronews Business.

“The lag can range from a few months to more than a year, depending on how the retail energy market is organised in each country.”

Many households are on fixed-price contracts, Mu said. Suppliers cannot pass on higher wholesale costs while those rates are fixed.

Suppliers also often buy gas and electricity in advance to protect themselves against price swings. That can delay the impact of wholesale price changes on household tariffs.

Higher bills could come in 2027

Mu said Europe’s benchmark wholesale gas price fell by 19% in the second half of 2025 compared with the first half of that year, and by 14% compared with the second half of 2024.

“I believe this is one of the key reasons behind the fall in household energy prices in the first half of 2026 despite the subsequent increase in wholesale gas prices following the conflict in the Middle East,” he said.

“For this reason, unfortunately, I do expect households could face higher energy bills in the second half of 2026, but more so in the first half of 2027,” he added.

Across EU capitals tracked by HEPI, household gas prices rose by 12% on average between 2 February and 1 September, while electricity prices rose by 4.2%.

HEPI’s October update recorded electricity price rises in 21 of the 33 European capitals it tracks, and gas price rises in 14 of the 27 capitals with gas data.

Regular trips to the park from birth to age 11 are linked to better mental health and social skills in children, a new study has found.

Going to the park can help children’s mental health and social skills as they grow up, according to a new study.

Researchers found that children who were taken to the park at least once a week from birth to the age of 11 scored, on average, 16.5% higher in their mental health assessments than those who visited less than once a week over the same period. The benefits remained even after adjusting for socioeconomic status and family problems.

“Parks give children space to be physically active, which is known to support mental and physical health, as well as helping adventurous and imaginative play to build confidence and independence,” said lead researcher Mark Ferguson of the University of Exeter in the United Kingdom.

“We believe parks could be more than places to play, but an important resource for children’s healthy development,” he added.

The study, published in the journal Epidemiology and Community Health, included 4,219 participants and focused on social-emotional development — the skills children need to manage their feelings, build relationships, behave appropriately and cope with everyday challenges.

Strong social-emotional development is an important foundation for good mental health in childhood and later life, the authors noted.

The study found that children tended to show better social-emotional development during periods when they went to parks more often. Children who visited parks more frequently overall also fared better than those who went less often.

Park visits were associated with improvements in both internalising behaviours, such as emotional symptoms and peer problems and externalising behaviours like conduct problems and hyperactivity or inattention.

Researchers also examined whether park visits and social-emotional development varied according to family background. Children from more advantaged areas appeared to visit parks more frequently at a younger age, while those from less advantaged families tended to visit more often as they grew older.

The study suggests parks and playgrounds could help reduce inequalities in children’s development, but only if they are easy for all families to use.

For parks to be beneficial, “communities need good-quality parks that are safe, accessible and welcoming to families from all backgrounds,” said Ferguson.

Because parks are free and open to everyone, they can have an “equigenic effect.” This describes how certain physical or social environments, most notably green spaces, can act as a levelling force that narrows health, psychological, or educational disparities between socioeconomic groups.

Scientists are mapping one of the world’s last wild ecosystems to help us ‘understand what we have lost elsewhere’.

Nesting turtles, fish-filled coral reefs, and mysterious deep-sea creatures: this is what scientists found in one of the world’s last largely untouched ecosystems.

Two remote coral atolls in the Pacific Ocean are being studied to support local and global conservation efforts.

Bikar and Bokak became the Marshall Islands’ first national marine sanctuaries in 2025. Since then, scientists have been working to establish a comprehensive ecological baseline for the 48,000-square-kilometre site, from sky to land and sea.

Their findings matter far beyond the remote atolls, which lie around 116 and 385 kilometres from the nearest inhabited atoll, respectively.

“They are among the best ecological reference systems we have to better understand what we have lost elsewhere and to provide fundamental insights needed for effective conservation and restoration efforts,” says marine ecologist Dr Alan Friedlander of the University of Hawai’i.

He served as chief scientist aboard a joint expedition in Bikar and Bokak with Pristine Seas, a global conservation and exploration project founded by National Geographic Explorer Enric Sala to help protect vital ocean areas.

What they found were “some of the most intact ecosystems remaining in the region” – and perhaps the world.

‘Treasures for the entire planet’: What the world can learn from remote ecosystems

Extensive monitoring of Bikar and Bokak in 2023 informed the creation of the protected area.

Researchers were guided by the Marshall Islands’ national framework for community-led conservation, which seeks to protect natural resources “while ensuring island life thrives for generations to come”, explains Friedlander, who led a recent study on the atolls’ ecosystems.

“Bikar and Bokak are not just treasures for the Marshall Islands but for the entire planet, a gift from the community of Utirik Atoll, which has traditionally and vigilantly safeguarded these fragile ecosystems for decades,” he says.

While the atolls have recently gained national protection, they have long been cared for through community-led stewardship, with high chiefs establishing ‘mo’ or ‘taboo’ areas. In these zones, human activity is restricted, allowing nature to rest and replenish – an approach that has been incorporated into the national framework.

It has resulted in an ecosystem that offers an unparalleled glimpse into how life functions with only minimal human influence.

“The Marshall Island government should be applauded for their foresight in protecting these global biodiversity hotspots, where human activity is distant and habitats teem with life,” says Friedlander. “As human activities increasingly threaten biodiversity, areas devoid of intense human impacts serve as vital refugia.”

Large marine protected areas like these are globally important benchmarks for understanding how tropical ocean ecosystems are structured and how they may change in an era shaped by human activity, the researchers say.

Remote atolls teem with life while wildlife is in decline elsewhere

Bikar and Bokak offer a rare contrast to most of the world. Monitored wildlife populations have fallen by an average of 73 per cent globally since 1970, according to WWF’s 2026 Living Planet Report, with marine populations down 59 per cent.

Bleaching-level heat stress hit 84 per cent of the world’s coral reefs between January 2023 and May 2025, and only around 3.5 per cent of the ocean is considered fully or highly protected.

Using scuba, underwater video, deep-sea cameras, and a submarine, Pristine Seas scientists explored Pacific ecosystems that, by contrast, remain relatively intact.

Across both atolls, they found 15 breeding or likely breeding seabird species and more than 260 kinds of reef fish, as well as open-water predators including sharks, jacks and wahoo. Cameras and a submarine also revealed “surprisingly diverse and poorly known deep-sea communities”, and two of the fish recorded might be new to science, the researchers say.

Nesting green sea turtles were also observed at Bikar.

Ecological differences between the two reefs were noted, although the researchers say the reasons are not yet clear. Bokak’s reefs are dominated by coral, with around twice the fish biomass of Bikar, where seaweed covers more than half of some deeper slopes.

The project also highlights the importance of assessing ecosystems in their entirety in order to conserve their integrity and track future climate-driven change, the researchers say, adding that future studies should examine nutrient transfer and ecological connectivity between habitats.

Even with responsible local governance, the most isolated tropical reef systems aren’t immune to the global impacts of human-caused climate change. They are increasingly affected by coral bleaching, ocean warming, sea-level rise, and changes in how much food the open ocean produces, the study warns.

The Happy Passports Index ranks 50 countries on everything from life satisfaction and civil liberties to passport strength and income, and the results are surprising.

A powerful passport might make it easier to see the world, but does it actually make you happier? A new ranking of 50 countries suggests the two don't always go hand in hand – but, often, they do.

The research behind the ranking, published by Global Citizen Solutions, a migration firm offering second residency and citizenship solutions, looked at 50 countries and how happy their residents are, how free they are at home, how far their passports travel and how well they live.

These cover everything from how people rate their lives and the civil liberties they enjoy to passport access, income, life expectancy and peace. The idea is to measure not just how easily people can travel, but how happy and free they are where they live.

All those factors added up to a score out of 100 in the Happy Passports Index ranking – and here’s what it shows.

Nordic nations come out on top

The Nordic nations are famous for the happiness of their residents, so it’s little surprise that they all come near the very top of the ranking.

Finland leads with 93.2 out of 100, and is closely followed by Iceland, with a score of 92.4 and Denmark, which was awarded 92.1.

Norway is in fourth, and Sweden comes in sixth place, with scores of 89.3 and 88.2, respectively.

Switzerland, another very wealthy nation with happy residents who boast strong passports, was in fifth, with a score of 88.3

Wealth and strong passports don’t necessarily mean a high placement in the ranking, though.

For instance, Singapore has the highest income and the longest healthy life expectancy as well as the strongest passport in the sample, but it only comes in at 10th place, held back by its wellbeing (23rd) and freedom at home (30th) scores.

The UK has a strong passport, which gives holders wide travel access, but it ranks 29th of 50 both on people’s sense of freedom to make life choices and on civil liberties. That equals a placement of just 17th in the overall ranking.

“The happiest countries tend to hold strong passports, but not always,” said Dr Laura Madrid, Lead Researcher at Global Citizen Solutions. “Among wealthier countries, our briefing finds that happiness correlates far more strongly with freedom than with passport strength. That is because a passport offers something different: choice beyond the border.”

More mobile, but not necessarily happier

Among wealthier countries, the index found that freedom to make personal choices was much more closely linked to life satisfaction than either passport strength or income.

Malta, Portugal, Japan, Cyprus, Malaysia, Spain and Greece all score well for passport access and healthy life expectancy, but their residents report lower levels of happiness.

All seven rank higher overall than they do for life satisfaction alone.

Portugal is a particularly striking example, coming 21st in the overall index despite ranking 39th for how people rate their lives.

The index’s findings suggest, then, that being able to travel widely doesn't automatically make life better at home.

Why balance matters more than wealth

New Zealand, Australia and Malta all make the top half of the rankings across most measures, despite falling outside the top ten for both wealth and passport strength. New Zealand, for example, ranks just 25th for income but eighth overall.

The common factor is a fairly even performance across the different measures, rather than excelling in just one.

That’s particularly clear for Costa Rica, Uruguay, Mexico, Panama, Brazil, Israel and Saudi Arabia, which all score highly for life satisfaction despite having less powerful passports, underlining that travel freedom is only one part of the picture.

At least two people have died, while others have been trapped in the rubble after a three-storey building collapsed in Brooklyn, New York, at the edge of a construction site on Wednesday afternoon.

Some 250 firefighters and police officers tackled the rubble with pickaxes and saws to pull people covered in dust from beneath piles of twisted wood and brick.

During a press conference, officials said that at least 17 people had been hospitalised, four in critical condition. While it is unclear whether people might still be trapped, New York City Fire Department officials stated that search and rescue operations would continue into the night.

“This has been an incredibly challenging and fast-moving situation, with precarious wreckage to navigate and dangerous voids beneath the surface,” Mayor Zohran Mamdani said. “This type of rescue is exactly what the FDNY trains for.”

According to New York City’s Buildings Commissioner, Ahmed Tigani, the building fell when construction workers were digging an empty lot next door for a new building. However, the cause of the collapse is under investigation.

The collapsed building, which housed apartments above ground-level businesses, was reduced to a massive mound of debris at the bottom of the construction pit. The neighbouring structure, which shared a wall with the building, was left standing but suffered extensive damage. Much of its exterior wall had been ripped away, leaving the interiors exposed, including a bedroom and closets with clothes still hanging inside.

One of the survivors was a woman who was pulled from the rubble by firefighters late in the afternoon after a hole had been dug through the debris. Meanwhile, more people continued to be pulled from the rubble as search and rescue operations proceeded, including seven children, although officials did not specify whether any of them were among the dead.

FDNY Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore said the rescue teams, who were digging by hand and using drones to carry out operations, were performing “dangerous and perilous” work. “Every move is choreographed,” she said.

One firefighter was left with minor injuries, according to fire officials.

One resident of the collapsed building, Anderson Velez, recounted that he was at work when his wife phoned and said that their two children, aged 2 and 7, were among those trapped in the rubble, the New York Post reported.

“She called me when the building collapsed while she was inside with rubble on top of her. She was screaming for someone to help get my son out and then the call cut off,” he said.
